sections.h2: Where is Paducah and what sets its housing market apart?
sections.html:
Paducah sits where the Tennessee River meets the Ohio River, roughly halfway between St. Louis and Nashville, and McCracken County runs its government from here. No other Jackson Purchase city is bigger, and the Paducah metro area, which reaches into Ballard, Carlisle and Livingston counties and Massac County in Illinois, held 103,481 people in 2020.

The city covers about 20 square miles of land. Settlers arrived around 1821, William Clark laid out the town in 1827, and the legislature incorporated it in 1838. Steamboat repair yards and the Illinois Central shops, completed in 1927, built the older neighborhoods that many sellers now own. A house here is usually tied to river history, which shows up in how buyers look at flood maps and old brick.

sections.h2: How common is home ownership in Paducah, and what does a house cost to carry?
sections.html:
QuickFacts counts 26,730 people in Paducah for July 2025, living in 11,741 households of about 2.19 people each. Homeowners hold 55.0 percent of those households, which leaves a lot of rental stock in town.

  • Typical home value over the 2020 to 2024 survey years: $165,300.
  • Monthly cost of owning: $1,323 with a mortgage and $519 without.
  • Typical rent: $834.
  • Household income: $49,915 at the median, with 22.3 percent of residents under the poverty line.

With values in that range, a roof or foundation bill can eat a big slice of the equity. Sellers in that spot often prefer a buyer who needs no lender inspection.

sections.h2: How did the Ohio River shape Paducah, and what does flood zoning mean for a seller?
sections.html:
The river's biggest test came in 1937. The Ohio crested at 60.8 feet on February 2, well past the 50 foot flood stage, and about 27,000 residents left their homes for nearly three weeks. Congress then had the Army Corps of Engineers build the flood wall that protects downtown today.

The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and regulates building inside Special Flood Hazard Areas under Chapter 50 of its code. Sixteen flood map panels cover the city. Anyone developing in a hazard area needs a permit application with a $100 fee, plans from a Kentucky registered engineer or architect, and a FEMA Elevation Certificate. The same certificate is what insurers use to price a policy, so a buyer's insurance agent may ask for it. Call the Engineering Department at 270-444-8511 to learn whether an address sits in a mapped zone.

sections.h2: Which Paducah neighborhoods and city rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
Lower Town is the oldest neighborhood. Most of its buildings date from after the Civil War, and since August 2000 the Artist Relocation Program has offered incentives for artists to buy and restore homes there. A twenty block stretch of downtown is a listed historic district.

  • Exterior changes visible from the street in the H-1 and H-2 historic zones need a Certificate of Appropriateness.
  • Tearing down a structure inside the Demolition Control Zone needs a demolition control permit, with the Planning Director, Chief Building Inspector and a historic commission chair signing off.
  • Occupancy of new or heavily renovated buildings requires a final inspection and a certificate of occupancy.
  • The Building Division at 270-444-8690 can confirm whether liens or fines are attached to a property address.

Make that call before choosing an asking price, because an open fine or unpermitted work can slow a closing.

sections.h2: How do Paducah's schools, roads and weather matter to buyers?
sections.html:
Two districts serve the city. Paducah Public Schools runs Clark, McNabb and Morgan elementary schools, Paducah Middle School and Paducah Tilghman High School. Parts of the city and the rest of the county fall under McCracken County Public Schools, which opened one consolidated county high school in August 2013. Check which district a house is zoned for before you advertise it.

Interstate 24 runs east to Nashville and west toward St. Louis, with a business loop through downtown, and Interstate 69 curves around the east side. Barkley Regional Airport offers regional jet service. The climate is humid subtropical, with roughly 50 inches of annual precipitation, 8.9 inches of snow and an occasional tornado outbreak, so buyers tend to ask about roof age and drainage.

sections.h2: How and when are McCracken County property taxes billed?
sections.html:
Kentucky fixes real estate values on January 1 each year, and the county's Property Valuation Administrator sets them. That office neither sets rates nor takes payment. Bills become payable at the Sheriff's office starting November 1, and a 2 percent discount applies when a bill is paid in full by that date. Payment without discount runs through December 31, a 5 percent penalty applies in January, and 10 percent applies after January 31 (KRS 134.015).

The Sheriff keeps open bills until April 15. They then pass to the County Clerk, where interest and penalty build at 1 percent a month, a lien goes on record, and a private investor may buy the bill at a yearly sale normally held in October. The County Attorney's office offers installment plans, and a bill on a current plan is marked unavailable for sale. A lien on file can hold up a closing until the balance is cleared.

sections.h2: Can a Paducah owner still appeal an assessment?
sections.html:
The 2026 appeal window has closed. Notices went out April 24, the last day to appeal to the PVA was May 18, the Clerk's filing deadline for the local assessment board was May 19, and the board met June 17. Each year follows a similar pattern, since the tax roll opens on the first Monday of May and stays open 13 days (KRS 133.045).

An owner starts by asking the PVA for a conference and brings recent neighborhood sales, an appraisal under two years old, or photos and a repair list for a condition appeal. If the conference fails, the owner files with the Clerk and a three person local panel rules. Anyone still unhappy can go on to the state's Board of Tax Appeals. Homeowners aged 65 or older and totally disabled owners can apply to the PVA for the homestead or disability exemption.

sections.h2: Which closing costs fall on a Paducah seller?
sections.html:
The seller pays Kentucky's deed transfer tax: $0.50 for every $500 of price, rounded up to the next $500 block, collected at the recording counter (KRS 142.050). A deed stating $165,300, the typical value above, owes $165.50. Foreclosure deeds, divorce transfers between spouses and nominal parent to child deeds are exempt.

sections.h2: Which selling route fits a Paducah house best?
sections.html: An agent listing reaches the most buyers but brings repairs, showings and a lender's timeline. Selling on your own saves the commission and hands you the marketing and paperwork. A cash offer from an investor skips repairs and appraisals, which can suit a house with flood history, a tired roof or an open code case. Add up what you would keep from each route after transfer tax, tax proration and any lien payoff.

faqs.q: Is Paducah in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of it are. The city maps Special Flood Hazard Areas on 16 FEMA map panels, and the Engineering Department at 270-444-8511 can tell you whether a specific address falls inside one. A mapped address can mean a buyer needs flood insurance, and an elevation certificate helps price that policy.

faqs.q: Which office collects Paducah's property tax bill?
faqs.a: Current bills are paid to the McCracken County Sheriff from November 1. The County Clerk takes over bills still open after April 15. Values come from the PVA, which handles no payments.

faqs.q: What happens to unpaid taxes when I sell?
faqs.a: Open taxes turn into a lien on record at the County Clerk, and the title company normally pays the lien out of your proceeds. Penalties run 5 percent in January and 10 percent after January 31, then 1 percent a month once the Clerk holds the bill. Request a payoff amount from the Sheriff or Clerk ahead of closing day.

faqs.q: Does tearing down an old building in Paducah take a permit?
faqs.a: Maybe. Inside the Demolition Control Zone you need a demolition control permit approved by city staff and a historic commission chair, and you bring redevelopment plans. Call Community Development at 270-444-8690 to check the zone for your address.

faqs.q: What does Kentucky's deed tax come to on a Paducah sale?
faqs.a: Fifty cents per $500 block of the price, so a $200,000 sale costs the seller $200. The clerk collects it as the deed is recorded, and KRS 142.050 exempts foreclosure deeds and certain family transfers.
